in_sanskrit.name: अत्रि
in_sanskrit.long_meaning: The name Atri is derived from the Sanskrit word अत्रि (Atri), which means 'boundless' or 'unending'. In Hindu mythology, Atri is the name of a sage and the father of the celestial nymphs, the Apsaras. He is also one of the seven great Rishis (sages) and is said to have performed severe penance to please Lord Shiva.

vedic_reference.note: Atri is a significant name in Hindu mythology and is mentioned in various Hindu scriptures. He is considered one of the seven great Rishis and is known for his penance and devotion to Lord Shiva. In the Vedas, Atri is mentioned as one of the sons of the sage Angiras and the goddess Svaha. He is also known as Atreya, and his hymns are found in the Rigveda.

data.cultural_impact: Atri is a name revered in Hindu culture for its connection to one of the ancient sages mentioned in the Mahabharata. This sage, Atri, was known for his wisdom and his role as a celestial parent to Draupadi, one of the central figures in the epic. The name holds a significant place in Hindu mythology and is a reminder of the sage-king rulers who governed and imparted knowledge during ancient times.
data.spiritual_significance: The name Atri holds deep spiritual significance in Hinduism, symbolizing wisdom, knowledge, and celestial parenthood. As a sage, Atri represents the quest for divine knowledge and understanding. The name also signifies a deep connection to the celestial beings, emphasizing the spiritual bond between the divine and the human realm. Remembering the spiritual lessons taught by sages like Atri can lead to personal growth and a deeper understanding of the divine.

historical_references.reference: Atri Muni was a sage mentioned in Hindu scriptures who is said to have visited Lord Rama during his exile in the forest. He was the guru of Bharata, Lord Rama's brother. Atri is also mentioned in the Mahabharata as a sage who performed a yajna (sacrifice) to please Indra.

Atri is also the name of an ancient city in India, believed to be located in the present-day state of Maharashtra. It is mentioned in the Rigveda as a place of religious significance, and was known for its connection to the goddess Amba. Later, it was a center of Buddhist learning and was visited by Chinese traveler Xuanzang during his travels in the 7th century CE.
